Buying a linen loincloth and putting it around his waist was a symbolic action by which Jeremiah showed how closely Yahweh had bound the people of Israel and Judah to himself. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Go and buy a linen loincloth for yourself and put it around your loins, to show how closely I have bound my people to myself]

A **linen loincloth** is a kind of undergarment made of cloth that a man wrapped around his waist and hips. If your readers would not be familiar with what a linen loincloth is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [a cloth undergarment made of linen]

The implication is that Yahweh is telling Jeremiah not to wash the loincloth. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [but do not let it get wet by washing it]

nt: Yahweh is using **arise** as a common expression of the culture to mean “set out to do something.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and set out and go to Perath]

The word **Perath** is the name of a place that is also referred to in verses 5–7. It is the same word that elsewhere is translated as “Euphrates.” This could refer to: (1) a place where there is a stream, mentioned in Joshua 18:23 as Parah, about 5 and a half kilometers (3.5 miles) northeast of Anathoth, which is about that same distance northeast of Jerusalem. It seems likely that Jeremiah traveled to this nearby place with a name that sounded very much like “Euphrates,” which would symbolize for him that great river of Babylon. (2) the Euphrates River, about 550 kilometers (350 miles) from Anathoth. Alternate translation: [the Euphrates River]

nt: Jeremiah is using **Give glory to Yahweh your God** as a common expression of the culture to mean “honor Yahweh your God.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Show honor to Yahweh your God]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the disaster that Yahweh will bring on the people were **darkness**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [before he brings a time of disaster]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the ruin that will come on the people were their **feet** stumbling on mountain paths in the dark. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he brings ruin on you while you are helpless in the growing dark]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the deliverance that the people hope for were **light**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you hope for deliverance]

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [but he turns it into utterly gloomy darkness]

x.ASV: But if ye will not hear it, my soul shall weep in secret for your pride; and mine eye shall weep sore, and run down with tears, because Jehovah’s flock is taken captive.
x.Darby: And if ye will not hear it, my soul shall weep in secret places for [your] pride; and mine eye shall weep sore, and run down with tears, because Jehovah's flock is gone into captivity.
x.KJV: But if ye will not hear it, my soul shall weep in secret places for your pride; and mine eye shall weep sore, and run down with tears, because the Lord’s flock is carried away captive.
x.YLT: And if ye do not hear it, In secret places doth my soul weep, because of pride, Yea, it weepeth sore, And the tear cometh down mine eyes, For the flock of Jehovah hath been taken captive.

nt: Jeremiah is presenting a possible condition, that the people of Judah will refuse to listen to what Yahweh says. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [But suppose you refuse to listen. Then my soul will weep in secret places]
Here, **my soul** represents I myself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I myself will weep]

Jeremiah is using **in secret places** as a common expression of the culture to mean “where no one else can see.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [where no one can see me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **pride**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your proud behavior]
The pronoun **she** refers to the soul of Jeremiah, which he mentions earlier in the verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and my soul will weep bitterly]

Jeremiah is repeating forms of the verb **weep** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [and she will weep bitterly]

The expression **has been taken captive** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [enemies have taken Yahweh’s flock captive]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the people of Judah were a **flock** of sheep that belongs to Yahweh. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s people have been taken captive]

x.ASV: Say thou unto the king and to the queen-mother, Humble yourselves, sit down; for your headtires are come down, even the crown of your glory.
x.Darby: Say unto the king and to the queen: Humble yourselves, sit down low; for from your heads shall come down the crown of your magnificence.
x.KJV: Say unto the king and to the queen, Humble yourselves, sit down: for your principalities shall come down, even the crown of your glory.
x.YLT: Say to the king and to the mistress: Make yourselves low--sit still, For come down have your principalities, The crown of your beauty.

nt: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Tell the king and to the queen mother to make themselves low, sit down]

The words “The Lord told me” are not in the text but are implied. This is the beginning of what Yahweh said to Jeremiah. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh said,]

Coming down from the throne and sitting on the ground was a symbolic action by which a king and a queen mother showed that they had been humbled and were mourning. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Come down from your thrones and sit on the ground to show that you are humbled and mourning]

The phrase **Make low! Sit!** expresses a single idea. The word **Make low** tells more about **Sit**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [Come down and sit humbly in the dust]

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **the crown of your glory** before the information about what has happened to it. Alternate translation: [for the crown of your glory has come down from your heads]
Here, **crown** represents royal authority. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your glorious royal authority]

it has been taken into exile

x.ASV: The cities of the South are shut up, and there is none to open them: Judah is carried away captive, all of it; it is wholly carried away captive.
x.Darby: The cities of the south are shut up, and there is none to open [them]; all Judah is carried away captive: it is wholly carried away captive.
x.KJV: The cities of the south shall be shut up, and none shall open them: Judah shall be carried away captive all of it, it shall be wholly carried away captive.
x.YLT: The cities of the south have been shut up, And there is none opening, Judah hath been removed--all of her, She hath been removed completely--

nt: The implication is that enemy armies will besiege these cities so that no one can go in or out of them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [The cities of the Negev are shut up by besieging armies, and no one can pass in or out of them]

The expression **are shut up** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Enemies have shut up the cities of the Negev]

The expressions **has been exiled** and **has been wholly exiled** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Enemies have carried away all of Judah, they have carried her away completely]

In this verse, the word **Judah** is singular in form, and Yahweh refers back to it with the singular pronoun **she**, but it refers to all of the people of Judah as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “Judah” and a plural pronoun. Alternate translation: [have been exiled, they have been wholly exiled]

x.ASV: Lift up your eyes, and behold them that come from the north: where is the flock that was given thee, thy beautiful flock?
x.Darby: Lift up your eyes, and behold them that come from the north. Where is the flock that was given thee, thy beautiful flock?
x.KJV: Lift up your eyes, and behold them that come from the north: where is the flock that was given thee, thy beautiful flock?
x.YLT: Lift up your eyes, and see those coming in from the north, Where is the drove given to thee, thy beautiful flock?

nt: The word **your** is plural here because Yahweh is addressing the people of Jerusalem, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Yahweh is using **Lift up your eyes** as a common expression of the culture to mean “look.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Look and see]

The implication is that **the ones coming from the north** are enemy armies that will invade the land. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the invading armies that are coming from the north]

Yahweh is using the question form to rebuke the leaders of Jerusalem for failing to care for the people whom he entrusted to them. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You have lost the flock given to you, your beautiful flock!]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the people of Judah were a **flock** of sheep that he had entrusted to their leaders. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people entrusted to you, your beautiful people]

The expression **given to you** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the flock that God gave to you]

x.ASV: What wilt thou say, when he shall set over thee as head those whom thou hast thyself taught to be friends to thee? shall not sorrows take hold of thee, as of a woman in travail?
x.Darby: What wilt thou say when he shall visit thee, since thou thyself hast trained them to be princes in chief over thee? Shall not sorrows take thee, as a woman in travail?
x.KJV: What wilt thou say when he shall punish thee? for thou hast taught them to be captains, and as chief over thee: shall not sorrows take thee, as a woman in travail?
x.YLT: What dost thou say, when He looketh after thee? And thou--thou hast taught them to be over thee--leaders for head? Do not pangs seize thee as a travailing woman?

nt: מַה־תֹּֽאמְרִי֙ כִּֽי־יִפְקֹ֣ד עָלַ֔יִ⁠ךְ וְ֠⁠אַתְּ לִמַּ֨דְתְּ אֹתָ֥⁠ם עָלַ֛יִ⁠ךְ אַלֻּפִ֖ים לְ⁠רֹ֑אשׁ

Yahweh is using the question form to warn the people of Judah about what is going to happen to them. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You will have nothing to say when he appoints over you those friends whom you, yourself, have taught, to be head over you!]

The pronoun **he** could refer to: (1) Yahweh, who will set foreign rulers over the people of Judah. Alternate translation: [the Lord sets over you] or (2) the enemy ruler who will appoint officials to rule over them. Alternate translation: [they set as head over you]
עָלַ֔יִ⁠ךְ וְ֠⁠אַתְּ לִמַּ֨דְתְּ אֹתָ֥⁠ם עָלַ֛יִ⁠ךְ אַלֻּפִ֖ים לְ⁠רֹ֑אשׁ

The implication is that the nations whom the people of Judah had cultivated as allies will become the rulers over them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [over you those whom you yourself taught to be your friends, making them rulers over you]
Here, **head** represents ruler. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to be ruler]
הֲ⁠ל֤וֹא חֲבָלִים֙ יֹאחֱז֔וּ⁠ךְ כְּמ֖וֹ אֵ֥שֶׁת לֵדָֽה

Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that great anguish will certainly come upon the people of Judah. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Surely labor pains will seize you like a woman in labor!]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a woman in labor** suffers sudden and severe pain, so the people of Judah will suffer great anguish. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [suddenly and severely, causing you great anguish]

x.ASV: And if thou say in thy heart, Wherefore are these things come upon me? for the greatness of thine iniquity are thy skirts uncovered, and thy heels suffer violence.
x.Darby: And if thou say in thy heart, Wherefore come these things upon me? For the greatness of thine iniquity are thy skirts uncovered, [and] thy heels have suffered violence.
x.KJV: And if thou say in thine heart, Wherefore come these things upon me? For the greatness of thine iniquity are thy skirts discovered, and thy heels made bare.
x.YLT: And when thou dost say in thy heart, `Wherefore have these met me?' For the abundance of thine iniquity Have thy skirts been uncovered, Have thy heels suffered violence.

nt: Yahweh is using **say in your heart** as a common expression of the culture to mean “think to yourself.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And if you ask yourself]

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [And when you ask yourself why these things have come upon you]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Because you have sinned so much]

The expressions **have been uncovered** and **have been exposed** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [your enemies have uncovered your skirts and exposed your heels]

Yahweh is referring to the sexual violation of the women of Judah in a polite way by using the phrases **your skirts have been uncovered** and **your heels have been exposed**. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [your women have been stripped naked and raped]

x.ASV: Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil.
x.Darby: Can an Ethiopian change his skin, or a leopard his spots? [Then] may ye also do good, who are accustomed to do evil.
x.KJV: Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil.
x.YLT: Doth a Cushite change his skin? and a leopard his spots? Ye also are able to do good, who are accustomed to do evil.

nt: Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that it is impossible for these people to change themselves. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [No Cushite can change the color of his skin, and no leopard can change its spots!]
The word **Cushite** is the name of a people group.

Yahweh actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what he is saying here. If a speaker of your language would not do that, you could translate the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Then, in the same way, you yourself are not able to do good, because you are accustomed to do evil]
The word **you** is plural here because Yahweh is addressing the people of Judah, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Yahweh is using the adjective **accustomed** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [you who are used to doing evil]

x.ASV: Therefore will I scatter them, as the stubble that passeth away, by the wind of the wilderness.
x.Darby: And I will scatter them as stubble that passeth away by the wind of the wilderness.
x.KJV: Therefore will I scatter them as the stubble that passeth away by the wind of the wilderness.
x.YLT: And I scatter them as stubble, Passing away, by a wind of the wilderness.

nt: The point of this comparison is that just as **stubble** is blown away helplessly by the wind, so the people of Judah will be scattered helplessly among the nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Therefore, I will scatter them helplessly, as helpless as bits of straw that the desert wind blows away]

The pronoun **them** refers to the people of Judah, whom Yahweh has been addressing directly in the previous verses. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Therefore, I will scatter you people of Judah]

The term **stubble** refers to the dry stalks that are left in a field after the grain has been harvested. If your readers would not be familiar with what stubble is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [like dry straw]

x.ASV: This is thy lot, the portion measured unto thee from me, saith Jehovah; because thou hast forgotten me, and trusted in falsehood.
x.Darby: This shall be thy lot, thy measured portion from me, saith Jehovah; because thou hast forgotten me, and confided in falsehood.
x.KJV: This is thy lot, the portion of thy measures from me, saith the Lord; because thou hast forgotten me, and trusted in falsehood.
x.YLT: This is thy lot, the portion of thy measures from Me--an affirmation of Jehovah, Because thou hast forgotten me, And dost trust in falsehood.

nt: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the punishment that he has determined for these people were a **lot** and a **portion** measured out to them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [This is what I have determined will happen to you, the punishment that I have assigned to you]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **portion** that is characterized by being measured out to these people. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the share that I have measured out for you]

Here, **a lie** represents false gods. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and trusted in gods that are not real]

x.ASV: Therefore will I also uncover thy skirts upon thy face, and thy shame shall appear.
x.Darby: Therefore will I also turn thy skirts over thy face, and thy shame shall be seen.
x.KJV: Therefore will I discover thy skirts upon thy face, that thy shame may appear.
x.YLT: I also have made bare thy skirts before thy face, And thy shame hath been seen.

nt: Here Yahweh is speaking as if he would publicly shame the people of Judah in the way that a man would **strip off** the skirts of a woman. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [So I myself shall expose you publicly]
The pronoun **I** refers to Yahweh, who is speaking here. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [So I, Yahweh, shall myself strip off]
See how you translated the similar expression in [6:7](../06/07.md).

Yahweh is referring to the exposure of these people’s nakedness in a polite way by using the phrase **your shame**. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [so that everyone will see you naked]

The expression **may be visible** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [so that people will see your shame]

x.ASV: I have seen thine abominations, even thine adulteries, and thy neighings, the lewdness of thy whoredom, on the hills in the field. Woe unto thee, O Jerusalem! thou wilt not be made clean; how long shall it yet be?
x.Darby: Thine adulteries, and thy neighings, the lewdness of thy fornication, on the hills, in the fields, — thine abominations, have I seen. Woe unto thee, Jerusalem! Wilt thou not be made clean? after how long a time yet?
x.KJV: I have seen thine adulteries, and thy neighings, the lewdness of thy whoredom, and thine abominations on the hills in the fields. Woe unto thee, O Jerusalem! wilt thou not be made clean? when shall it once be?
x.YLT: Thine adulteries, and thy neighings, The wickedness of thy whoredom, on heights in a field, I have seen thine abominations. Woe to thee, O Jerusalem, Thou art not cleansed, after when is it again?

nt: נִֽאֻפַ֤יִ⁠ךְ וּ⁠מִצְהֲלוֹתַ֨יִ⁠ךְ֙ זִמַּ֣ת זְנוּתֵ֔⁠ךְ עַל־גְּבָעוֹת֙ בַּ⁠שָּׂדֶ֔ה

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [I have seen your adulteries and your neighings, the lewdness of your harlotry on the hills in the fields]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the worship that these people give to other gods were **adulteries** that they commit against him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Your unfaithful worship of other gods]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the desire that these people have for other gods were the **neighings** of animals that want to mate. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and your lustful cravings for other gods]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the worship that these people give to idols were **harlotry**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the shameful way you worship idols]

By **the lewdness of your harlotry**, Yahweh means the shameless and disgusting behavior of Israel’s idol worship, comparing it to the sexual acts of a prostitute. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [your disgusting behavior of acting like a prostitute]

The implication is that these people worshiped idols at shrines that were on these hills. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [at the shrines on the hills in the fields]

Here, **your abominations** represents the idols that these people worship, which Yahweh detests. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your worship of the detestable idols]

Yahweh is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of sorrow over the judgment that is coming on Jerusalem. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [How terrible it will be for you, Jerusalem]

Yahweh is using the question form to rebuke the people of Jerusalem for refusing to purify themselves. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You have refused to become clean for far too long!]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if being morally pure were being **clean**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you refuse to become morally pure]
